sections.title: From Concrete to Abstract (0:00-1:00)
sections.content: Transition from geometric vectors in R² (arrows) to the abstract definition. Emphasize that a vector space is not just 'arrows', but any set of objects that obey the same 'rules of engagement' (linearity). Prerequisite: Familiarity with 2D/3D coordinate systems.
sections.example: Visualize an arrow moving in a 2D plane vs. a list of numbers [x, y] shifting positions.

sections.title: The Eight Axioms: The Rules of the Game (1:00-2:30)
sections.content: Introduce the two main operations: Vector Addition and Scalar Multiplication. Use a split-screen animation showing standard geometric vectors on the left and abstract algebraic structures (like polynomials) on the right, highlighting that they both satisfy the same structural axioms (Commutativity, Associativity, Identity, Inverse, Distributivity).
sections.example: Imagine a 'Vector Robot' that moves based on arrows, and a 'Polynomial Robot' where 'adding' means combining coefficients. Show they both follow the same rule: A + B = B + A.

sections.title: Beyond Arrows: Diverse Vector Spaces (2:30-4:00)
sections.content: Demonstrate that vector spaces are everywhere. Focus on Function Spaces. Show how a set of continuous functions can be treated as vectors. Use a graphical overlay: a sine wave 'stretching' and 'adding' like a geometric vector.
sections.example: A cat (Vector A) and a dog (Vector B). If we combine them, we get a 'super-pet' (A+B) that obeys the same algebraic laws as the arrows, even if they aren't geometric shapes.

sections.title: The Power of Abstraction (4:00-5:00)
sections.content: Summarize why we care: By proving a property for an 'abstract vector space', we automatically prove it for matrices, polynomials, and signals. Close with the visualization of a 'Unified Mathematical Map' where disparate concepts meet.
sections.example: A device controller that uses the same logic to tune audio signals (waves) as it does to rotate a 3D character in a video game (matrices).
